title: Agentic Symbolic Search: Characterizing PDEs Beyond Hand-crafted Expressions, Meshes, and Neural Networks
authors: Zongmin Yu, Liu Yang
abstract: Mathematicians understand a PDE solution through mathematical structures rather than tables of computed values. Historically, this has been the product of mathematical analysis, carried out by hand for each problem individually. Neither numerical simulation nor neural networks produce those structures directly. We propose Agentic Symbolic Search (ASYS), a prior-guided framework in which an agent translates PDE theory, public problem constraints, and accumulated search experience into testable differentiable symbolic programs. The mathematical forms are refined under evolutionary search, while their continuous parameters are fit by gradient-based optimization. This makes the search an automated form of inductive-bias injection rather than blind symbolic regression. For problems with known analytical forms, ASYS recovers these forms naturally; for other problems, ASYS constructs analytical approximations which can guide mathematicians toward further analysis. In our experiments, across five problems spanning bounded dynamics, finite-time blow-up, and free-boundary focusing, ASYS produces interpretable representations, including a geometric interface formula for Allen-Cahn 2D dynamics and a nine-parameter contraction law for Keller-Segel chemotactic blow-up, in settings where no closed-form description was previously available. ASYS shows the possibility of a new paradigm for characterizing PDE solutions, beyond handcrafted analytical solutions, mesh-based numerical solutions, and neural network approximations.

infographic.key_insight: Agentic Symbolic Search (ASYS) combines PDE theory, prior constraints, and evolutionary search to discover interpretable symbolic formulas for PDE behavior, rather than only numerical or neural approximations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: ASYS could help engineers obtain compact, human-readable surrogate laws for complex PDE systems, supporting analysis, design decisions, and downstream control or simulation workflows.
method: Agent uses PDE theory, problem constraints, and past search experience to propose testable symbolic programs.
Evolutionary search refines the mathematical structure of candidate expressions.
Gradient-based optimization fits continuous parameters in the discovered formulas.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five PDE problems spanning bounded dynamics, finite-time blow-up, and free-boundary focusing, the method recovered known analytical forms when available and produced new interpretable formulas when closed forms were unknown.
infographic.watch_item: The approach may be sensitive to the quality of prior guidance and search settings, so results could depend on problem-specific constraints and optimization stability.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic Symbolic Search: Characterizing PDEs Beyond Hand-crafted Expressions, Meshes, and Neural Networks

title: Evolutionary Two-Stage Hyperparameter Optimization Strategies for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
authors: Fedor Buzaev, Dmitry Efremenko, Egor Bugaev, Andrei Ermakov, Denis Derkach, Daria Pugacheva
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) solve Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) by embedding physical laws into neural network training. However, their performance suffers from unstable convergence, training plateaus, and strong sensitivity to architectural and optimization hyperparameters due to the highly non-convex and multi-term structure of the physics-informed loss. In this setting, the outer-loop hyperparameter search is a noisy and black-box optimization problem over heterogeneous parameters, where classical local or gradient-based strategies are easily trapped in suboptimal regions. Evolutionary algorithms, with their population-based exploration and ability to handle mixed, non-differentiable search spaces, provide a more robust mechanism for discovering promising configurations. We propose and investigate a two-stage approach based on evolutionary algorithms that combines exploration and exploitation parts of PINNs training to improve solution accuracy and robustness under fixed computational budgets. In the first stage, we perform low-fidelity training runs with truncated epochs to rapidly screen candidate configurations, treating hyperparameter selection as a black-box outer-loop problem. In the second stage, only the most promising candidates are fully trained with standard gradient-based optimizers to refine the solution. Evaluated on three popular problems, namely Advection, Klein-Gordon and Helmholtz equations, our method consistently outperforms standard training and achieves significantly lower mean error within constrained computational resources.

infographic.key_insight: A two-stage evolutionary hyperparameter search can make PINNs more accurate and robust by using cheap low-fidelity screening before full gradient-based training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical way to improve PDE-solving PINNs under fixed compute budgets when standard training is unstable or highly sensitive to hyperparameters.
method: Use an evolutionary algorithm to search mixed PINN hyperparameters in a noisy black-box outer loop.
Run short truncated training to quickly evaluate and filter candidate configurations.
Fully train only the best candidates with standard gradient-based optimizers in a second stage.
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach was evaluated on Advection, Klein-Gordon, and Helmholtz problems and reported consistently lower mean error than standard training under constrained computational resources.
infographic.watch_item: Low-fidelity screening can mis-rank candidates, so the method depends on choosing a truncation budget that preserves correlation with final performance.
infographic.paper_title: Evolutionary Two-Stage Hyperparameter Optimization Strategies for Physics-Informed Neural Networks

title: HEPTv2: End-to-End Efficient Point Transformer for Charged Particle Reconstruction
authors: Siqi Miao, Shitij Govil, Jack P. Rodgers, Mia Liu, Javier Duarte, Shih-Chieh Hsu
abstract: Charged-particle tracking -- reconstructing trajectories from sparse detector measurements -- is a fundamental high-energy-physics inference problem and a canonical example of learning under extreme combinatorial ambiguity. At the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC), tracking must remain accurate and efficient despite unprecedented collision densities. Graph neural networks perform strongly, but incur substantial costs from graph construction and processing, while transformer-based approaches rely on auxiliary stages that prevent end-to-end optimization. To address this, we present HEPTv2, an end-to-end point-transformer architecture that reconstructs tracks from detector hits in one trainable pipeline. HEPTv2 combines a locality-aware point encoder with a track decoder that predicts complete trajectories without graph-building, clustering, or filtering. The encoder uses locality-sensitive hashing in detector coordinate space to preserve tracking-relevant geometry while enabling efficient local attention. The decoder resolves ambiguities through sectorized decoding and direct hit-to-track prediction under joint encoder-decoder supervision, allowing the full pipeline to be optimized end-to-end. On TrackML, HEPTv2 achieves 98.6% double-majority tracking efficiency at a 0.8% fake rate, while requiring only $\sim$15~ms inference time and 0.4~GB peak memory per event on a NVIDIA A100 GPU. Latency and memory scale approximately linearly for events with up to $5\times10^5$ hits. HEPTv2 establishes a new state of the art in the accuracy-latency trade-off, improving efficiency by 4.5% over the strongest prior transformer and by 1.1--2.2% over optimized graph-based pipelines, while reducing latency by factors of 7 and 38--52, respectively. These results show end-to-end transformers can deliver the accuracy and efficiency required for real-time particle reconstruction at the HL-LHC.

infographic.key_insight: HEPTv2 is an end-to-end point-transformer that reconstructs charged-particle tracks directly from detector hits without graph building, clustering, or filtering.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It targets real-time, high-throughput tracking at the HL-LHC by improving the accuracy-latency trade-off while keeping memory and inference cost low on GPU hardware.
method: Locality-aware point encoder with locality-sensitive hashing in detector coordinate space
Sectorized track decoder with direct hit-to-track prediction
Joint encoder-decoder supervision for end-to-end optimization
infographic.evidence_signal: On TrackML, the model reports 98.6% double-majority tracking efficiency at a 0.8% fake rate, with about 15 ms inference time and 0.4 GB peak memory per event on an NVIDIA A100.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on carefully tuned sectorization and locality hashing, which could affect robustness when detector conditions or hit densities change.
infographic.paper_title: HEPTv2: End-to-End Efficient Point Transformer for Charged Particle Reconstruction

title: UltraQuant: 4-bit KV Caching for Context-Heavy Agents
authors: Inesh Chakrabarti, David Limpus, Aditi Ghai Rana, Bowen Bao, Spandan Tiwari, Thiago Crepaldi
abstract: Context-heavy agents place unusual pressure on the key-value (KV) cache: long prefixes are reused across many short turns, while concurrency determines whether the serving system can keep GPUs utilized. We study 4-bit KV-cache compression for this setting, using TurboQuant-style rotation and codebook quantization as a quality anchor and vLLM FP8 KV caching as the deployment anchor. We report three contributions. First, we frame 4-bit KV caching around multi-round agent workloads where task quality, cache residency, and serving throughput must be measured jointly. Second, we describe the practical design choices needed to make the 4-bit path robust, including asymmetric K/V treatment, Walsh-Hadamard rotation, QJL removal, and block-scale variants. Third, we present serving optimizations on AMD GPUs, including optimized decode-attention kernels and UltraQuant, an FP4 approximation path that uses FP8 queries, FP4 KV tensors, UE8M0 group scales, and native scaled-MFMA support on CDNA4. On a long-context, multi-turn agentic workload, UltraQuant cuts P50 time-to-first-token by 3.47x in the cache-pressured late rounds (2.3x across all rounds) and raises output throughput by 1.63x over the FP8 KV baseline.

infographic.key_insight: UltraQuant shows that 4-bit KV caching can preserve agent quality while substantially improving latency and throughput in long-context, multi-turn workloads.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For serving context-heavy agents, KV-cache compression is not just a memory optimization but a systems-level lever for keeping GPUs busy and reducing time-to-first-token under concurrency.
method: Use 4-bit KV-cache quantization tailored to multi-round agent traces
Apply rotation/codebook techniques with asymmetric K/V handling, Walsh-Hadamard rotation, and block-scale variants
Deploy AMD GPU serving optimizations, including optimized decode-attention kernels and an FP4 UltraQuant path with FP8 queries and UE8M0 group scales
infographic.evidence_signal: On a long-context, multi-turn agentic workload, UltraQuant achieved a 3.47x P50 time-to-first-token improvement in cache-pressured late rounds and 1.63x higher output throughput versus the FP8 KV baseline.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on specialized kernel support and hardware features, so portability and stability across different GPU platforms may be a practical constraint.
infographic.paper_title: UltraQuant: 4-bit KV Caching for Context-Heavy Agents

title: Software package MaRDI Open Interfaces for improved interoperability in numerical optimization
authors: Dmitry I. Kabanov, Stephan Rave, Mario Ohlberger
abstract: To address the challenges of interoperability in computational science, we present the latest updates to the software package MaRDI Open Interfaces. This software package aims to decrease the time and coding/testing efforts spent by computational scientists on tasks such as writing bindings to numerical solvers and adapting experiment codes to the varying interfaces of solvers for the same problem type (e.g., for benchmarking, which solver is better). By streamlining these tasks, this software package helps researchers focus on the actual essence of their computational projects. Here, we demonstrate a recently developed interface for nonlinear optimization and illustrate how it can be applied for computational experiments with optimization problems. As an example of such problem, we consider training of physics-informed neural networks to predict the solutions of viscous Burgers' equation.

infographic.key_insight: MaRDI Open Interfaces reduces the integration burden between computational experiments and nonlinear optimization solvers by providing a common interface layer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This improves interoperability, making it easier to swap, benchmark, and bind numerical solvers without rewriting experiment code.
method: Updated software package with a new nonlinear optimization interface
Supports computational experiments by standardizing solver access
Demonstrated on training physics-informed neural networks for viscous Burgers' equation
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a demonstration on optimization-based experiments for physics-informed neural networks, but does not provide quantitative benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: Utility depends on how well the interface covers solver-specific features and whether adapting legacy codes still requires nontrivial integration work.
infographic.paper_title: Software package MaRDI Open Interfaces for improved interoperability in numerical optimization

title: Interpretable Meta-Learning for Multi-Objective Chemical Search
authors: Antonio Varagnolo, Yulia Pimonova, Michael G. Taylor, Raphaël Pestourie, Nicholas E. Lubbers
abstract: Navigating the vast space of synthetically accessible molecules demands surrogate models that are interpretable and capable of handling multiple competing objectives at the same time. Deep learning approaches struggle to satisfy them under the computational constraints of quantum-level chemistry. Here, we introduce a modular pipeline that combines interpretable linear meta-learning models and adaptive-confidence uncertainty quantification into an Efficient Global Optimization (EGO) framework for multi-objective molecular discovery. For the first time, linear meta-learning is deployed in a multi-objective chemical search setting: by training across chemical objectives and cheap auxiliary properties, the meta-learned surrogates acquire transferable chemical knowledge that adapts rapidly to new objectives from limited data. Evaluated empirically on a real large scale search for spin-crossover metal-organic complexes, the baseline performs 78% worse in Pareto sense than the meta-learning alternative. We also address the calibration challenges inherent to active search. Since optimal candidates typically lie precisely in the distributional tails, standard uncertainty estimates fail. We introduce an adaptive confidence-tuning algorithm that dynamically recalibrates the exploration-exploitation trade-off as the molecular search evolves. Empirically, dynamic confidence tuning further dominates over 50% of the statically calibrated front.

infographic.key_insight: A modular meta-learning plus adaptive-confidence EGO pipeline can make multi-objective molecular search more interpretable, data-efficient, and better at finding Pareto-optimal candidates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a practical surrogate-model framework for computational chemistry workflows where quantum-level evaluations are expensive and multiple competing design goals must be balanced.
method: Train interpretable linear meta-learners across chemical objectives and cheap auxiliary properties to transfer chemical knowledge.
Embed the surrogates in an Efficient Global Optimization loop for multi-objective molecular discovery.
Use adaptive confidence tuning to recalibrate uncertainty during active search and adjust exploration vs. exploitation over time.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a large-scale spin-crossover metal-organic complex search, the baseline is reported to be 78% worse in Pareto performance, and dynamic confidence tuning outperforms more than 50% of the statically calibrated front.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on reliable uncertainty calibration and may be sensitive to how auxiliary properties and confidence updates are chosen during search.
infographic.paper_title: Interpretable Meta-Learning for Multi-Objective Chemical Search

title: LLM agent safety, multi-turn red-teaming, jailbreak benchmarks, adversarial robustness, safety-critical systems
authors: Hanwool Lee, Dasol Choi, Bokyeong Kim, Seung Geun Kim, Haon Park
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed as supervisory components for safety-critical systems, yet their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure remains poorly characterized. We present NRT-Bench, a benchmark for multi-turn red-teaming of LLM agents acting as operators of a safety-critical system, instantiated in a simulated nuclear power plant control room. A five-role operator team, each backed by a configurable LLM, runs a plant governed by six critical safety functions (CSFs), while adversaries inject messages over four channels in bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is an objective signal rather than LLM-judged text: a run terminates the moment any CSF is lost, attributed to the causing message. Evaluating four frontier operator models under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol, we find that adaptive multi-turn attacks reliably push the operator team past a safety limit: across the four models, between 8.7% and 12.1% of attack sessions end with the plant losing a critical safety function. Although the four models look almost equally robust by this aggregate rate, their failures barely overlap: of $149$ sessions, none defeat all four models while a third defeat at least one, so vulnerabilities are nearly disjoint across models rather than nested. The effect of added defences is strongly model-dependent: the same guardrail stack or safety-advisor agent that lowers attack success for one model can raise it for another. We release the simulation venue, attack dataset, and replay tooling for reproducible safety evaluation of LLM agents.

infographic.key_insight: Multi-turn, adaptive red-teaming can reliably drive LLM-operated safety-critical systems past a safety limit, and the resulting vulnerabilities differ sharply across models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For safety-critical deployment, robustness must be tested under sustained adversarial interaction, because a defense that helps one LLM operator may hurt another.
method: NRT-Bench simulates a nuclear power plant control room with a five-role LLM operator team and six critical safety functions.
Adversaries attack through four channels over bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback.
A run ends immediately when any critical safety function is lost, and the triggering message is recorded as the cause.
infographic.evidence_signal: In paired-replay evaluation of four frontier operator models, 8.7%–12.1% of attack sessions caused loss of a critical safety function, and the 149-session failures were largely non-overlapping across models.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from a simulated control-room benchmark, so real-world transfer, operator integration, and defense side effects need careful validation before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: LLM agent safety, multi-turn red-teaming, jailbreak benchmarks, adversarial robustness, safety-critical systems

title: AutoPass: Evidence-Guided LLM Agents for Compiler Performance Tuning
authors: Zepeng Li, Jie Ren, Zhanyong Tang, Jie Zheng, Zheng Wang
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for code compilation tasks, but applying them to runtime performance tuning is difficult due to complex microarchitectural effects and noisy runtime measurements. We present AutoPass, a multi-agent framework for compiler performance tuning that uses compiler and runtime evidence to guide LLM-generated optimization decisions. Rather than treating the compiler as a black box like prior auto-tuning schemes, AutoPass opens up the compiler to the LLM, enabling it to query compiler-internal optimization states and analyze the intermediate representation to orchestrate compiler options. The search process iteratively refines optimization configurations using measured runtime feedback to diagnose regressions and guide latency-improving edits. AutoPass operates in an inference-only, training-free setting and requires no offline training or task-specific fine-tuning, making it readily applicable to new benchmarks and platforms. We implement AutoPass on the LLVM compiler and evaluate it on server-grade x86-64 and embedded ARM64 systems. AutoPass outperforms expert-tuned heuristics and classical autotuning methods, achieving geometric-mean speedups of 1.043x and 1.117x over LLVM -O3 on x86-64 and ARM64, respectively.

infographic.key_insight: AutoPass improves compiler performance tuning by letting LLM agents use compiler-internal and runtime evidence to iteratively choose better optimization settings instead of guessing from a black-box compiler.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical, training-free way to automate compiler optimization across new benchmarks and hardware targets with minimal manual retuning.
method: Multi-agent LLM framework for compiler performance tuning
Queries LLVM internal optimization states and intermediate representation
Uses runtime feedback to diagnose regressions and refine optimization configurations iteratively
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on LLVM for server-grade x86-64 and embedded ARM64, AutoPass achieved geometric-mean speedups of 1.043x and 1.117x over LLVM -O3.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on noisy runtime measurements and compiler-internal signals, so stability and generalization may vary across workloads and platforms.
infographic.paper_title: AutoPass: Evidence-Guided LLM Agents for Compiler Performance Tuning

title: What Do Safety-Aligned LLMs Learn From Mixed Compliance Demonstrations?
authors: Sihui Dai, Mann Patel
abstract: Prior work has shown that in-context demonstrations can jailbreak language models, but it remains unclear how models interpret different types of compliance demonstrations. We study this by mixing benign compliance demonstrations (non-harmful request, helpful response) with harmful compliance demonstrations (harmful request, helpful response) and testing three hypotheses about how demonstration composition drives harmful compliance. Across four models, we find that benign and harmful demonstrations are not interchangeable: benign demonstrations can either reduce or increase harmful compliance depending on the model. We further show that preference optimization is the critical training stage that prevents benign demonstrations from increasing harmful compliance, that demonstration ordering exhibits strong recency bias, and that models differ in how refusal interacts with in-context learning: some adopt demonstrated formatting even when refusing, while others override all in-context signals upon refusal. Taken together, this work moves beyond showing that demonstration-based jailbreaking works to characterizing how it works: what models extract from compliance demonstrations depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training methodology.

infographic.key_insight: Safety-aligned LLMs do not treat benign and harmful compliance demonstrations the same: the effect on harmful compliance depends on demonstration content, ordering, and training stage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For prompt and safety design, this means in-context examples can unintentionally increase jailbreak risk, so demonstration selection and order should be treated as safety-critical controls.
method: Mixed benign compliance demos with harmful compliance demos
Tested three hypotheses across four models
Compared effects of ordering, refusal behavior, and training stage
infographic.evidence_signal: The study evaluates mixed in-context demonstrations across four models and uses harmful-compliance outcomes to compare benign versus harmful demo effects.
infographic.watch_item: Results may not transfer universally across all model families or prompt settings, so relying on benign examples without testing could create hidden jailbreak risk.
infographic.paper_title: What Do Safety-Aligned LLMs Learn From Mixed Compliance Demonstrations?

title: Marginal Advantage Accumulation for Memory-Driven Agent Self-Evolution
authors: Mingyu Yang, Keye Zheng, Congchao Cheng, Yujie Liu, Xingkang Lu, Fan Jiang
abstract: In batch-style trace distillation, the same memory operation may receive contradictory feedback across different batches. Existing methods lack a cross-batch, operation-level evidence accumulation mechanism, making it impossible to distinguish stably effective operations from accidental hits. This paper formalizes the requirement as two structural conditions, alignability and comparability, and proposes Marginal Advantage Accumulation (MAA). MAA constructs differential signals to make them comparable across batches, accumulates signed evidence per operation via EMA, and ensures cross-batch traceability through semantic identity merging. As a post-processing architecture, MAA achieves the best results in 14 out of 16 settings across 4 benchmarks and 4 target models, consistently outperforming existing batch-level distillation baselines and matching or surpassing online alternatives in most settings, while reducing optimization-phase token consumption by approximately 75%.

infographic.key_insight: Marginal Advantage Accumulation (MAA) turns inconsistent batch-level memory feedback into comparable, cross-batch evidence so stable operations can be separated from accidental wins.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For memory-driven agent training, MAA offers a post-processing way to improve trace distillation quality while cutting optimization-phase token use by about 75%.
method: Build differential signals so operation feedback is comparable across batches
Accumulate signed per-operation evidence with EMA to track consistent advantage
Merge semantically identical traces to preserve cross-batch traceability
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 4 benchmarks and 4 target models, MAA achieved the best results in 14 of 16 settings, outperforming batch-level baselines and usually matching or exceeding online alternatives.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on reliable semantic identity merging and well-defined operation-level alignment, which may be sensitive to trace quality and implementation details.
infographic.paper_title: Marginal Advantage Accumulation for Memory-Driven Agent Self-Evolution

title: Contagion Networks: Evaluator Bias Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
authors: Zewen Liu
abstract: When large language models serve as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases propagate through the agent network. We introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring how evaluator biases spread across interacting LLM agents. In a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), we measure the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Gamma_3 and find that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (gamma in [0.157, 0.352]), even within the same underlying model. We identify three propagation regimes governed by the spectral radius rho(Gamma_N), and demonstrate that homogeneous-model agents produce contagion coefficients 3-5x weaker than cross-model coefficients observed in prior work (MM-EPC: gamma approx 0.85-1.3), placing them in the suppression regime. We show that increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%, providing an actionable mitigation strategy. We release the open-source Contagion Network experimental framework.

infographic.key_insight: Evaluator bias in multi-agent LLM systems can spread from one agent to others like contagion, even when all agents use the same underlying model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Designing evaluator committees and bias-aware agent networks can materially reduce error propagation, with a 3-member committee cutting effective contagion by 72.4%.
method: Defined Contagion Networks to measure how evaluator bias propagates across interacting LLM agents.
Ran a controlled 3-agent experiment with DeepSeek-chat under three evaluator bias profiles: structured, balanced, and evidence-based.
Computed the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix (Gamma_3) and analyzed propagation regimes via the spectral radius rho(Gamma_N).
infographic.evidence_signal: In the 3-agent study, contagion coefficients remained nonzero at gamma = 0.157 to 0.352, while increasing committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduced effective contagion by 72.4%.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from a controlled setup on one model family, so real-world multi-model systems may show different propagation strength and dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: Contagion Networks: Evaluator Bias Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems

title: Agentic AutoResearch forSpace Autonomy: An Auditable, LLM-Driven Research Agent for Aerospace Control Problems
authors: Amit Jain, Richard Linares
abstract: Spacecraft guidance, navigation, and control functions are increasingly realized as learned policies distilled from expert solvers. Developing such a policy is itself a research process: an investigator selects an architecture and hyperparameters, runs experiments, and must determine whether an apparent improvement is genuine or merely seed noise. This paper presents AutoResearch, a framework in which a large language model autonomously drives that loop for aerospace control problems, coupled with a credibility layer, built into the loop, that certifies each reported result against the problem's own measured seed noise. The language model serves only as the offline research agent that develops the control policy; the trained policy it produces is then deployed onboard the spacecraft, while the model itself never operates the vehicle. At each iteration the agent reads a plain-language problem description and the run history, proposes a single edit to the training script, executes it, and logs the outcome. No reported result is credited until it passes the same three checks: measured per-problem seed noise, reseeded verification of the best configuration, and leave-one-out pruning of the agent's edits. The same loop is applied, unchanged, to two aerospace control problems: a Clohessy-Wiltshire relative rendezvous and a safety-constrained collision-avoidance docking past a keep-out zone, each calibrated against a known optimal control benchmark. In both, the audited policy clears the measured seed noise by many standard deviations; an undirected search over the same parameters does not. On the docking problem the gap becomes categorical: undirected search yields no feasible policy, while the learned policy stays outside the keep-out zone on every seed.

infographic.key_insight: AutoResearch uses an LLM as an offline research agent to autonomously iterate on aerospace control training, while an embedded credibility layer only accepts results that exceed measured seed noise and pass verification checks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a reproducible way to discover and audit spacecraft guidance and control policies, helping engineers distinguish real gains from seed-dependent noise before deployment.
method: LLM reads a plain-language problem description and experiment history, then proposes one training-script edit per iteration.
Each candidate policy is evaluated with measured per-problem seed noise, reseeded verification of the best setting, and leave-one-out pruning of the agent’s edits.
The same audited loop is applied to two spacecraft control tasks: Clohessy-Wiltshire rendezvous and constrained docking around a keep-out zone.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across both problems, the audited policies outperform measured seed noise by many standard deviations; on the docking task, the learned policy remains feasible on every seed while undirected search finds no feasible policy.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on accurate seed-noise calibration and problem-specific benchmarking, so its credibility claims may weaken if the evaluation protocol or task dynamics change.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic AutoResearch forSpace Autonomy: An Auditable, LLM-Driven Research Agent for Aerospace Control Problems

title: Structuring and Tokenizing Distributed User Interest Context for Generative Recommendation
authors: Ruizhong Qiu, Yinglong Xia, Dongqi Fu, Hanqing Zeng, Ren Chen, Xiangjun Fan
abstract: Generative recommendation is an emerging paradigm that has shown promise in industrial recommendation systems, aiming to predict users' next interactions from their historical behaviors. At the core of generative recommendation lies item tokenization, which bridges item semantics and recommendation models. However, existing methods often struggle to effectively organize and inject complex user-behavioral and item-semantic contexts into recommendation models simultaneously. On the one hand, existing graph-based integration methods, such as graph serialization and graph neural networks, either suffer from scalability issues or exploit only local graph information. On the other hand, existing semantic tokenization methods typically rely on heuristics and lack explicit supervision signals, which may lead to inaccurate or suboptimal semantic representations. To address these limitations in user interest context modeling, we propose G2Rec, a scalable framework that unifies holistic graph-based user co-engagement modeling with semantic tokenization for industrial-scale generative recommendation. Overall, G2Rec enables recommendation models to capture holistic and semantically grounded user interest prototypes without requiring ground-truth user interests, thereby providing more comprehensive and accurate modeling of user behavior contexts in industrial sequential recommendation. Online deployment across product surfaces and extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of G2Rec over existing methods.

infographic.key_insight: G2Rec unifies global user co-engagement structure and semantic tokenization to produce more accurate user interest prototypes for generative recommendation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach is designed for industrial-scale sequential recommendation, making it relevant for large recommender systems that need scalable context modeling.
method: Builds a holistic graph-based model of user co-engagement across interactions.
Tokenizes item semantics with explicit supervision signals to avoid heuristic-only representations.
Combines graph structure and semantic grounding into a unified generative recommendation framework.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper reports online deployment across product surfaces and extensive experiments on public datasets showing superiority over existing methods.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment may require careful handling of scalability, graph construction cost, and the quality of learned semantic tokens in changing production data.
infographic.paper_title: Structuring and Tokenizing Distributed User Interest Context for Generative Recommendation

title: SSH-Net: A Deep Neural Network for Predicting Failure Time Distribution Functions under Competing Risks with Application to GPU Data
authors: Jie Min, Yueyao Wang, Mengkun Chen
abstract: Competing risks are commonly observed in engineering fields and can bring challenges to time-to-event data modeling when the application scenarios are complicated. Recently, deep neural networks have received great attention for prediction with competing risks, due to their flexibility and high learning capability. However, the complexity of neural network structure brings extra difficulty in hyperparameter tuning based on different data inputs. Additionally, when an engineered system has complex physical structures with multiple hierarchical levels, treating all structural levels as a single group of inputs may fail to capture critical information. To address the issues, we propose a Structured Segmented Hazard Deep Neural Network (SSH-Net) for failure time prediction under cause-specific competing risks framework. Our approach associates neural network structure with data structures, and allows different covariate groups to impact the failure prediction through separate sub-networks. The neural network is constructed based on a cause-specific competing risks model. The SSH-Net outputs cause-specific hazard functions, and utilizes the penalized log-likelihood as the loss function. The prediction accuracy of SSH-Net is validated through simulation studies by evaluating the Brier score, the area under receiver operating characteristic curves (AUC), and the root mean square error (RMSE) of the predicted cause-specific cumulative incident function. We further demonstrate the model's ability to predict failure time distribution functions using the Titan GPU failure time data.

infographic.key_insight: SSH-Net links neural-network architecture to grouped covariates so it can predict cause-specific failure-time distributions under competing risks more effectively.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It is useful for complex engineered systems where hierarchical structure matters, such as GPU reliability analysis and other multi-cause failure problems.
method: Uses a structured segmented neural network with separate sub-networks for different covariate groups.
Formulates prediction within a cause-specific competing-risks framework and outputs cause-specific hazard functions.
Trains with a penalized log-likelihood loss to estimate failure-time distribution functions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper validates performance with simulation studies using Brier score, AUC, and RMSE, and demonstrates applicability on Titan GPU failure-time data.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on careful grouping and tuning of sub-networks, so poorly chosen structure or hyperparameters could reduce predictive benefit.
infographic.paper_title: SSH-Net: A Deep Neural Network for Predicting Failure Time Distribution Functions under Competing Risks with Application to GPU Data

title: Statistical Properties of Training & Generalization
authors: Itay Lavie, Noam Levi, Yonatan Kahn
abstract: Deep learning has managed to evade numerous intuitions from classical statistics to achieve unprecedented performance on a number of real-world tasks. In this article, we investigate the key features and surprises of deep learning from a physics-informed perspective, taking care to point out and justify where possible the many choices inherent in constructing a deep learning model. In particular, we review the phenomenon of neural scaling laws and discuss their interplay with the constraints and inductive biases which may be present when applying machine learning to problems in physics.

infographic.key_insight: Deep learning can defy classical statistical intuition, and its performance is strongly shaped by scaling behavior plus the inductive biases built into the model and problem setup.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For scientific machine learning, this means model choices, physics constraints, and data scaling strategy are not secondary details but central design variables that affect generalization.
method: Review neural scaling laws from a physics-informed perspective
Analyze how inductive biases and constraints influence training and generalization
Justify the modeling choices involved in deep learning for physics applications
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper is a review and synthesis of observed deep learning behavior and scaling phenomena, rather than a new benchmark study reported in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions depend on how models are constructed and constrained, so results may not transfer directly across tasks without careful problem-specific tuning.
infographic.paper_title: Statistical Properties of Training & Generalization

title: Execution-State Capsules: Graph-Bound Execution-State Checkpoint and Restore for Low-Latency, Small-Batch, On-Device Physical-AI Serving
authors: Liang Su
abstract: Mainstream LLM serving systems reuse prefix work mainly through paged or radix key-value (KV) caches. This is highly effective for high-throughput, high-concurrency serving, but it manages only one positional fragment of execution state: the KV cache. We study the opposite regime: low-latency, small-batch, on-device physical-AI serving, where interactive LLM agents, speech systems, and robot policies repeatedly branch, reset, interrupt, and re-enter under tight responsiveness budgets. We introduce execution-state capsules, a graph-bound checkpoint and restore mechanism for the complete restorable state at a committed boundary. FlashRT is a white-box, backend-facing kernel runtime whose evaluated NVIDIA CUDA backend runs captured graph plans over contiguous static buffers with no block-table indirection. Because the live state is a closed set of named buffers, a capsule can snapshot, restore, fork, or roll back the whole execution boundary, including KV, recurrent state, convolution state, MTP state, and metadata. This moves reuse from token-addressed KV fragments to graph-bound execution-state boundaries. On an RTX 5090, capsule restore is byte-exact at the stored-state level and token-identical under greedy decode. A KV-only ablation diverges, showing that recurrent state is load-bearing. GPU-resident snapshot and restore are sub-millisecond, and TTFT speedup over cold prefill grows from 3.9x at 2k tokens to 27x at 16k tokens. On Jetson AGX Thor and DGX Spark, the same correctness and structural properties hold. Capsules are not a replacement for high-throughput KV-cache serving; they define a complementary latency-first serving point for explicit execution-state reuse.

infographic.key_insight: Execution-state capsules generalize reuse from KV-cache fragments to the entire graph-bound execution state, enabling fast checkpoint/restore for low-latency, small-batch on-device AI serving.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is useful for interactive agents, speech models, and robot policies that frequently branch, interrupt, and resume under tight responsiveness budgets.
method: Capture the complete restorable state at a committed graph boundary
Store live state in contiguous static buffers with no block-table indirection
Restore/fork/roll back KV, recurrent, convolution, MTP, and metadata state together
infographic.evidence_signal: On RTX 5090, restore is byte-exact and greedy-decoded outputs are token-identical; GPU-resident snapshot/restore is sub-millisecond and TTFT speedup rises from 3.9x at 2k tokens to 27x at 16k tokens.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on a white-box runtime and backend-facing graph capture, so integration may be harder than standard KV-only serving stacks.
infographic.paper_title: Execution-State Capsules: Graph-Bound Execution-State Checkpoint and Restore for Low-Latency, Small-Batch, On-Device Physical-AI Serving

title: Multi-LCB: Extending LiveCodeBench to Multiple Programming Languages
authors: Maria Ivanova, Pavel Zadorozhny, Rodion Levichev, Ivan Petrov, Adamenko Pavel, Ivan Lopatin
abstract: LiveCodeBench (LCB) has recently become a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on code-generation tasks. By curating competitive programming problems, constantly adding fresh problems to the set, and filtering them by release dates, LCB provides contamination-aware evaluation and offers a holistic view of coding capability. However, LCB remains restricted to Python, leaving open the question of whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering. We introduce Multi-LCB, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs across twelve programming languages, including Python. Multi-LCB transforms Python tasks from the LCB dataset into equivalent tasks in other languages while preserving LCB's contamination controls and evaluation protocol. Because it is fully compatible with the original LCB format, Multi-LCB will automatically track future LCB updates, enabling systematic assessment of cross-language code generation competence and requiring models to sustain performance well beyond Python. We evaluated 24 LLMs for instruction and reasoning on Multi-LCB, uncovering evidence of Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and substantial disparities in multilingual performance. Our results establish Multi-LCB as a rigorous new benchmark for multi-programming-language code evaluation, directly addressing LCB's primary limitation and exposing critical gaps in current LLM capabilities.

infographic.key_insight: Multi-LCB extends LiveCodeBench from Python-only evaluation to 12 programming languages, revealing how poorly many LLMs generalize across languages.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The benchmark helps engineers assess whether code models are truly deployment-ready for multilingual software development, not just Python tasks.
method: Transforms LiveCodeBench Python problems into equivalent tasks in 11 additional languages
Preserves contamination filtering, release-date controls, and the original evaluation protocol
Automatically stays compatible with future LiveCodeBench updates
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors evaluated 24 LLMs and found evidence of Python overfitting, language-specific contamination, and large performance gaps across languages.
infographic.watch_item: Because tasks are translated from Python, benchmark quality depends on preserving semantic equivalence and language-specific idioms accurately.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-LCB: Extending LiveCodeBench to Multiple Programming Languages

title: Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents
authors: Alaia Solko-Breslin, Pramod Kaushik Mudrakarta, Mihai Christodorescu, Somesh Jha, Krishnamurthy Dj Dvijotham
abstract: Securing AI agents that operate in complex digital environments has become a critical need, and runtime monitoring approaches that formulate and enforce policies expressed in a formal language like Datalog offer a promising solution. However, existing approaches are restricted to deterministic policies. In many practical applications of AI agents, there is a need to enforce security policies in the face of ambiguity, leading to probabilistic predicates or state transitions (for example, a declassifier or Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detector that has some failure probability on each invocation). Furthermore, in many such applications, one cannot easily make the independence assumptions necessary to invoke prior work on probabilistic inference in Datalog. We address this by introducing a sound and efficient framework for such verification based on distributionally robust optimization, computing sound upper bounds on the probability of policy violation regardless of possible correlations between predicates. On standard benchmarks for terminal and tool calling agents, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms prior art and improves the security-utility trade-off while ensuring rigorous bounds on the probability of policy violation.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a sound probabilistic verification framework for AI agent policies that upper-bounds violation risk even when probabilistic predicates may be correlated.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables practical runtime security monitoring for AI agents in uncertain environments, improving the security-utility trade-off without relying on unrealistic independence assumptions.
method: Formulate policy verification for probabilistic Datalog-style rules as a distributionally robust optimization problem.
Compute sound upper bounds on policy-violation probability under arbitrary correlations between probabilistic predicates.
Target runtime monitoring for security policies involving uncertain components such as PII detectors or declassifiers.
infographic.evidence_signal: On standard benchmarks for terminal and tool-calling agents, the method outperforms prior art while providing rigorous bounds on policy-violation probability.
infographic.watch_item: Soundness depends on the conservativeness of the bound, so tighter guarantees may come with some loss in utility or extra runtime cost.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents

title: Quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for PDEs
authors: Xiang Rao, Yuxuan Shen
abstract: We develop QCPIKAN, the first quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold network designed to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). Built upon Chebyshev-polynomial KAN layers and parameterized quantum circuits, this hybrid framework embeds physical constraints into the training loss to enforce physical consistency. Our theoretical investigations grounded in approximation theory prove that this design accelerates high-frequency error convergence to an exponential rate and effectively mitigates numerical dispersion. We validate the framework across three typical seepage scenarios in porous media, including single-phase flow, component transport and two-phase flow. Compared with existing quantum-classical physics-informed neural networks, QCPIKAN achieves superior performance in global prediction accuracy, local error control, dynamic evolution tracking and displacement front localization. This work provides a robust and efficient alternative for solving complex PDEs.

infographic.key_insight: QCPIKAN combines Chebyshev-polynomial Kolmogorov-Arnold networks with parameterized quantum circuits to solve PDEs while enforcing physics through the loss function.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a hybrid quantum-classical solver that can improve accuracy and stability for porous-media simulations and other PDE-heavy engineering workflows.
method: Uses Chebyshev-based KAN layers as the classical backbone for function approximation.
Integrates parameterized quantum circuits into a physics-informed training framework.
Adds PDE residual and physical-constraint terms to the loss to enforce consistency.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation on three seepage problems in porous media—single-phase flow, component transport, and two-phase flow—showing better global accuracy, local error control, dynamic tracking, and displacement-front localization than prior quantum-classical PINNs.
infographic.watch_item: As a hybrid quantum-classical model, training and deployment may be sensitive to circuit design, optimization stability, and hardware/noise constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum-classical physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for PDEs

title: Shifting-based Optimizable Linear Relaxations for General Activation Functions
authors: Philipp Kern, László Antal, Erika Ábráham, Carsten Sinz
abstract: The use of neural networks (NNs) is rapidly increasing, including in safety- and security-critical domains. To provide formal guarantees about NN behavior, many verification methods rely on optimizable linear relaxations of activation functions. However, existing techniques depend on hand-crafted relaxations for each activation function. Extension to state-of-the-art activation functions therefore requires substantial manual effort. In contrast, our approach SLiR (Shifting-based Linear Relaxations) is broadly applicable, requiring only a Lipschitz constant or a set of critical points. SLiR parameterizes relaxations by their slope and computes the corresponding offset via a shifting procedure that ensures sound upper and lower bounds over the input domain, enabling efficient optimization while maintaining correctness. Our experiments show that SLiR produces tight relaxations across a wide range of practical activation functions and enables verification of up to 7.8x more properties compared to state-of-the-art methods.

infographic.key_insight: SLiR makes linear relaxations for neural-network activations broadly optimizable by computing sound bounds through slope-based shifting, rather than relying on activation-specific hand-crafted formulas.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This reduces manual effort when verifying modern neural networks and helps formal methods scale to new activation functions used in safety- and security-critical systems.
method: Parameterize each relaxation by its slope.
Compute the offset with a shifting procedure to preserve sound upper and lower bounds.
Use only a Lipschitz constant or critical points to support general activation functions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments in the abstract report tight relaxations across many practical activation functions and up to 7.8x more verifiable properties than state-of-the-art methods.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on correctly obtaining a valid Lipschitz constant or critical points, and soundness can be compromised if these inputs are inaccurate.
infographic.paper_title: Shifting-based Optimizable Linear Relaxations for General Activation Functions
